https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: There was no evidence of third-party involvement in Nicholas Brandram’s death, the coroner said. Photograph: Family handout/PA View image in fullscreen There was no evidence of third-party involvement in Nicholas Brandram’s death, the coroner said. Photograph: Family handout/PA London Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case was found dead after missing family meal, inquest hears Brother-in-law went to check on Nicholas Brandram at his London home and found him unresponsive, coroner says Press Association Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.13 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The man who was arrested on suspicion of being the so-called “Putney pusher” was found dead at his home after missing a family meal, an inquest has heard. Nicholas Brandram, 44, was arrested in June in connection with an incident on Putney Bridge on 5 May 2017 in which a jogger shoved a woman headfirst into the path of an oncoming bus. The former banker was found unresponsive inside his home in Chiswick, west London , on 15 September. Melanie Lee, the area coroner, opened and suspended an inquest into his death at west London coroner’s court on Tuesday afternoon. Opening the proceedings, she said: “On the evening of Tuesday 15 September 2026, Nicholas did not attend a family meal as planned. “His brother-in-law attended Nicholas’s home address and gained access using a spare key provided by a neighbour. Upon searching the house, he found Nicholas in an upstairs room. “Paramedics attended and despite resuscitation, he was pronounced deceased at 8.58pm.” The coroner said the death was not considered suspicious and there was “no evidence of third-party involvement”. Lee said provisional results from a postmortem examination indicated his death was “due to ligature compression of the neck”. The Metropolitan police has referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) over its contact with Brandram, who was released under investigation after his arrest. The force said on 17 September that its investigation into the Putney Bridge incident remained ongoing after Brandram’s death. Lee said on Tuesday: “I have been informed this afternoon that a referral has been made to the IOPC. On that basis, I am suspending the inquest.” The coroner added that an inquest was not a trial and “nobody and no organisation is on trial”. Brandram’s sisters, who were present at the inquest opening, have previously accused police of failing him and wider society. The coroner told the family: “I offer my sincere condolences for your loss. I appreciate today will not be an easy day for you.” The family have said they believe Brandram took his own life after “months of immense pressure” caused by the Met’s investigation. In an interview with BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Brandram’s sisters Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker said he did not match the description of the attacker. Hicks said there had been “urgency” by the Met to arrest Brandram and to have that reported in the press. “I think he couldn’t understand why there wasn’t urgency to help clear his name,” she added. https://www.surinenglish.com/malaga/axar.text: The father of an 11-year-old boy with autism who has been in care since June tried to set himself alight in Malaga city to protest against the situation. The man allegedly doused himself with petrol and threatened to light a match at the Canal Sur radio and television studio on Sunday 6 September. The incident happened at around 6pm when the man arrived at the studio on a motorbike and asked for help in English. According to sources, he intended to gain access to the building so that the regional television station could broadcast his situation. However, when he failed to do so, he allegedly grabbed a bottle of petrol and, in front of the entrance, poured the liquid over himself. National and Local Police officers along with firefighters and medical services arrived at the scene and the area was cordoned off. An employee of Canal Sur took on the role of negotiator thanks to his fluency in English. According to sources, his intervention was crucial in calming the man down and diverting his attention to prevent him from setting himself alight.The firefighters deployed high-pressure hoses and the police then stepped in to subdue him. Meanwhile, paramedics administered medication to calm him down and took him to hospital. His lawyer confirmed that the man only suffered minor burns and said, "he is calmer now; it was an act born of the helplessness of a father who felt overwhelmed. He did not want to take his own life, but it was an act of desperation."The 50-year-old Romanian man has recently spoken to SUR about the legal action the family is taking to try to regain custody of their son , who had been taken away by the Andalusian regional government's social services in June. The decision followed an accident which happened in April and reports received from UK social services relating to the boy's situation when the family was living there.UK social servicesOn 28 April the boy fell from a first-floor window in Rincón de la Victoria and but was caught by an awning while in the care of his 17-year-old sister. This incident was compounded by reports sent from the United Kingdom on 11 May regarding alleged lack of supervision and irregular school attendance during his stay in the country, as well as a subsequent inspection of the home in which officials from the Andalusian regional government noted organisational and hygiene shortcomings. As a result, on 5 June, the regional office for social inclusion agreed to take the boy into provisional care.The implementation of this measure led to the child being removed on 9 June following an interview with his mother, a process which the parents have questioned due to the lack of an interpreter and the abrupt manner in which it was carried out. On 16 June, the child was transferred to a care centre in Albox (Almeria province), a location more than 200 kilometres from his home, which makes it difficult to comply with the fortnightly visiting arrangements, the family claims.Against this backdrop, on 29 July, the family filed a formal appeal against the decision to place the boy in care at a court in Malaga city. The appeal denies the serious neglect or negligence, considers the decision to to pu the boy into care to be a "disproportionate" measure and calls for the child to be returned to the family home. The proceedings are currently pending the three-month legal deadline set by the Andalusian Law on children and adolescents for a final ruling to be issued, while the parents’ legal representatives have also brought the matter to the attention of the Andalusian Ombudsman.Meanwhile, the care home management reported in July that the child was making positive progress, noting improvements in toilet training, medication management and his adaptation to the care home.More reporting from the Axarquía area

https://www.dw.com/en/hungarys-reckoning.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NSk6 Prime Minister Peter Magyar addresses an extraordinary session of the National Assembly on Monday Image: Zsolt Szigetvary/MTI/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement One of the new Hungarian government's key pledges was to investigate corruption under Viktor Orban , recover embezzled assets, and hold those responsible accountable . Or, in the words of Prime Minister Peter Magyar, it is time to "liquidate Orban's mafia state." During his election campaign, Magyar had already announced a "program for the road to prison." As prime minister, he launched "Operation Purgatory" at the end of June 2026. Measured against his fighting talk, little has happened so far. There have been no sweeping purges of the state apparatus, although some government funds flowing to Orban-aligned businessmen have been cut off. Police and prosecutors have summoned a handful of relatively unknown individuals for questioning, and a few people were arrested. The governing majority also established an agency to recover assets, but it is is not yet up and running. But at the beginning of the week, Hungarians witnessed the first significant development in the promised reckoning with the Orban system. Two prominent lawmakers and former ministers were arrested over corruption allegations. On Monday, Magyar's Tisza Party parliamentary faction used its two-thirds majority to lift the immunity of two lawmakers from the opposition Orban camp: Balazs Hanko, formerly minister for culture and innovation and a lawmaker from Orban's Fidesz party, and Miklos Sesztak, a former development minister who is now a lawmaker for the small Christian Democratic People's Party (KDNP), which has been a Fidesz affiliate since 2010. Both are the subject of corruption investigations. Former Minister Miklos Sesztak in 2017 Image: Robert Szaniszlo/ZUMA/IMAGO Illegal party financing, bribery Balazs Hanko was not among those in Orban's system who enriched themselves on a large scale. But he is seen as a symbol of the common practice under Orban of systematically using public money to fund the ruling party, Orban's network of allies, election campaigns, and propaganda efforts. Specifically, as minister, Hanko allegedly unlawfully allocated around 50 million euros from the National Cultural Fund (NKA), which he oversaw, in 2025 and 2026, including funds intended for election campaign purposes. The case of Miklos Sesztak is different. He is one of the wealthiest lawmakers in Hungary and has made headlines for more than a decade with his personal corruption scandals — another typical trait of the Orban system. As minister, Sesztak allegedly accepted around €30 million ($34 million) in bribes with an accomplice between 2015 and 2018. The alleged payments involved contracts related to the state-owned Hungarian bus company Volanbusz and the construction sector. Barricaded in parliament with his family Sesztak went straight to the prosecutor's office on Monday after his immunity was lifted, where he was taken into pretrial detention. Balazs Hanko took a different route. He arrived at Parliament on Monday morning with his wife and four teenage children and, after his immunity was lifted, said he was waiting for the authorities to make a decision. In practice, it appeared that he was barricading himself inside. Only after Parliament Speaker Agnes Forsthoffer formally ordered Hanko in writing that evening to leave the building, and he received a summons from the prosecutor's office, did he finally head for the exit, accompanied by his family and Fidesz lawmakers protesting what they called Magyar's "arbitrary rule." The entire episode was livestreamed on Viktor Orban's Facebook page. After Hanko said goodbye to his family outside, a misunderstanding occurred. His SUV driver, apparently believing Hanko was already inside the vehicle, drove off without him. Hanko ran after the SUV, and the livestream on Orban's Facebook page then cut out. Later that evening, Hungarian media reported that Hanko had also been placed in pretrial detention. Balazs Hanko talks to press after walking out of the National Assembly Image: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance Prime Minister Magyar's immunity lifted Earlier that afternoon, Prime Minister Peter Magyar delivered a sharp speech in Parliament on the two cases. His own immunity had also been lifted beforehand — over a case that is classified in the records as theft. In June 2024, Magyar took a phone from a man who had been filming him without permission at a nightclub and threw it into the Danube, where it was later found. Magyar had explicitly asked for his immunity to be lifted in the case. It is a calculated PR move intended to show that the same standards apply to everyone. But it is also a risky maneuver — if convicted, Magyar could lose his seat in Parliament. In his parliamentary speech, he offered Fidesz and KDNP lawmakers a stark comparison: "How many hundreds of thousands of phones would you have to throw into the Danube to come close to the trillions allegedly stolen by the Fidesz-KDNP mafia?" Dispute over Prosecutor General Magyar has also spoken forcefully about Hungary's justice system. He has praised rank-and-file judicial employees while criticizing the leadership of the prosecutor's office, accusing them of repeatedly covering up corruption cases as "collaborators of the Orban system." At the center of the dispute is a fight over the appointment of a new prosecutor general. The Tisza faction rejected Zoltan Szathmary, the candidate proposed by President Andras Baka, because his brother works for the Office for Constitutional Protection and, in that role, is a suspect in an ongoing politically sensitive case known as the "Gold Convoy" affair. In March 2026, Viktor Orban ordered the detention of a legal Ukrainian money shipment. The escorts were arrested in dramatic fashion, and cash and gold bars were seized. Orban and other Fidesz politicians indirectly accused Magyar's Tisza Party of receiving funding from Ukraine . Several people involved in the operation are now under investigation for abuse of office. Orban himself is not currently part of the proceedings but could be in the future. How much Orban influence remains in Hungary's politics? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Hungarians seek a swift reckoning Although Magyar has formally emphasized the independence of the judiciary, his comments in the current debates have given the impression that he is getting ahead of judicial decisions or becoming too deeply involved. At the same time, expectations among many Hungarians for a swift reckoning are high — and public debate's often return to the topic of how people want to "hear the handcuffs click." A recent poll found that a large majority of Hungarians consider the former Orban order "systemically corrupt" and a "mafia state." Overall, Magyar and his government face the challenge of balancing the rule of law with public expectations. Many former critics of Orban are also calling for the reckoning with the Orban system to be handled properly. Prominent attorney Gyorgy Magyar, for example, who represented people in numerous human rights and rule-of-law cases under Orban, called for "prudence, patience, calm, discipline, and professionalism" in an interview with the news outlet Hirklikk. Questions remain about whether "Operation Purgatory" will be merely spectacle, or whether the justice system will investigate corruption cases independently and in keeping with the rule of law. https://english.news.cn/europe/20261014/.text: First U.S. rotational troops arrive in Lithuania VILNIUS, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The first U.S. troops of a new rotational deployment have arrived in Lithuania, President Gitanas Nauseda announced on Tuesday, marking the resumption of American troop rotations in the Baltic country. Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said in September that two U.S. battalions were expected to arrive by the end of October, bringing the American military presence in Lithuania back to more than 1,000 personnel, broadly in line with previous deployments. More than 1,000 U.S. troops and their military equipment began leaving Lithuania in early June following the completion of their rotation. The arrival of their replacements was subsequently delayed as Washington reviewed its military presence in Europe. U.S. forces have conducted rotational deployments in Lithuania since 2014, with heavy battalion rotations beginning in 2019. The latest arrival follows U.S. President Donald Trump's remarks last week that Washington would consider establishing a permanent U.S. military base in Lithuania. Nauseda welcomed the possibility, while Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said Lithuania was prepared to accommodate permanently stationed American troops and cover the costs of establishing a base if Washington agreed. ■ News In-depth Sports Business Culture World China Regions Asia & Pacific Europe Middle East North America South America Africa Organizations Services Weather Live & Work in China Doing Business Investment Visit China Study in China More Special Reports Photos Video Corrections About Us Contact Us Media Qiushi Journal Taiwan.cn Youth.cn GMW.cn CE.cn Ecns.cn China Daily CRI.cn China.org.cn People's Daily
